title: On Duality
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the Bodhipakshika Dharma, a list of seven lists that makes up thirty-seven aids to awakening, and asks how to hold steps to take alongside a wholeness already present. Nomon reads the opening of Dogen's Fukanzazengi with its "and yet," then Diana Winston's Wide Awake, where Ajahn Buddhadasa's "little nirvana" and Hakuin's line on awakening to one's own nature sit beside the slow weeding of greed, hatred, and delusion. Nomon also pictures the Buddha as a doctor and describes how language divides the world into this or that. The evening closes with standing chants and prostrations that recite the thirty-seven aids.

sentences.text: I really appreciated the comments of everyone who was able to be here.
Last year we had a big meeting to look at what we're doing together.
We had the foil of this decision about what time to meet, but it really seemed to bring in a lot more than just what time.
What are we really trying to do together?
Why do we come or not come?
There seemed to be a tremendous sort of energy of commitment to our life and to the practice.
It was really great.
Maybe in the end it won't change a thing, but just having the meeting was great.
I also want to thank again; I think four people gave talks while I was not on sabbatical this summer.
So far, I've listened to some of Edie's talk on the Eightfold Noble Truth and some of John's talk on preferences, and I'm looking forward to hearing what Kate and Joan said, I think.
I haven't listened yet.
What I've heard, the talks I've heard so far, were great—so practical and grounded and straightforward that through the format and the forms and the meditation we do, we access something mysterious.
There certainly does seem to be a feeling or a sense that there's more to this life than what we can talk about or understand.
It's so helpful to have some way of being with that together.
Yet it's easy to misunderstand this whole process as if it were all mysterious and impossible to understand.
You have to be like a high holy person or go to a monastery for twenty years to do more than just play around.
So I appreciated John and Edie's talks being very practical, and I'm hoping to follow in their excellent examples and be a little bit more practical.
There are things we can do, teachings that come to us through the tradition that are really helpful for each of us.
They'll be expressed or understood a little differently because we can only express things through our own life, right?
Our own experience.
You can't express something through somebody else's life.
We also had a speaker on Saturday who was the same way, very accessing the mystery, but also very practical.
Anita Feng from Blue Heron Zen Community, which is a Korean Zen practice center, came.
It was wonderful how many similarities there were.
It was the same feeling and the same way of talking about the Dharma, even though it came from a different cultural tradition.
Of course, she's a white Jewish lady from New England, and she loves that about herself.
Actually, she was telling me before we were chatting a little bit before, she said, "I love that how much I blend in, nobody would know."
She's like one below the highest level in their system, a pretty important person in the Korean Zen world.
She just dresses normally and looks like a Jewish grandmother from New England, which she is.
We can look at, we often use the metaphor of path, right?
Of the path.
The path doesn't do you much good if you don't walk on it, right?
It's nice that there's a path and we can appreciate the path and have nice pictures of the path, interesting calligraphies of the path, and read books about the path.
But then the path is outside, you know.
So we actually have to walk.
How do we walk?
In a literal way, it's nice that Bob could come tonight because he is taking some people walking starting on Friday.
They're going to walk silently around Mount Rainier, one hundred miles.
I wonder how many steps that is.
He should send you with a pedometer; I'll probably max it out.
To try to take each step, you know, each step of that journey as a step on the path.
Seven people signed up.
Isn't that amazing?
Never done this before.
So thank you to Bob for being nutty enough to say yes to that.
You never know who's going to respond, right?
That's the other thing about walking on the path: if you take a step on the path, you don't know.
We think we're so self-focused, right?
Think about it, we're so self-focused.
We think about, "Well, is this good for me?"
But then we step onto the path because we think it's good for us, and maybe it is.
But then maybe we look over our shoulder and we see, "Oh, we helped somebody else take a step on the path."
So we talked about that when we were talking about what time to practice last week.
It was wonderful.
Quite a few people said, "Well, this is a little better for me, but more important is what's better for you."
So it's beautiful.
Tonight I wanted to introduce a collection of teachings, a way, a possible way of engaging the Buddhist path.
It's a list of lists.
As you know, the Buddhist teachings were famous for their lists, partly because of the way they survived in oral form for so many centuries, way longer than America has been in existence.
Monks and nuns recited this—I don't know how many volumes, this huge amount of material—kept it alive just from memory.
It's easy to remember something if it's a list of eight, because then you can just check yourself, "Well, at least it's seven.
Wait a minute."
So Buddhism is famous for its lists.

To us, lists don't have quite the same feeling as they might have had for somebody who was doing a recitation practice and saying this list, reciting this list, chanting this list, devoting themselves to this list.
I've always assumed there would have been different monks or nuns who would specialize in different parts of the material, because how else would they?

When we look at a list, we usually see it on paper, and it pretty much looks like a to-do list to us, which we do not have such spiritual associations with, probably, because what is the nature of a to-do list?
Failure, right?
That's the nature of a to-do list.
We can learn to live with that and appreciate that and understand that that's not a problem, but that's a strong association.
So we see this Buddhist list, and we know, "Uh-oh, we're doomed for failure."
In Edie's talk, you must have put up a chart or something, which is good; it was a list.
You said something like on paper, it just looks kind of dead, you know?
You have to bring it to life.
The teaching I want to bring up is called—it has a fancy-sounding name, which I like the name, we will enjoy it.
The name is Bodhi Pakshika Dharma, the name in Sanskrit for this list of lists.
It's a list of seven lists, and it comprises thirty-seven steps, thirty-seven points.
Not exactly thirty-seven things in our to-do list, but thirty-seven things we could attend to and practice with.
The way it's understood is that it's both sequential and circular at the same time, and each one of the thirty-seven somehow includes the other thirty-six.
I don't know what the right adjective is for that; we probably don't have an English adjective for that because we don't believe in that, you know, that one thing could include everything else.
Maybe that's ecology.
That's ecology.
It's maybe not the best list; there's, I'm sure, other lists, and you could probably make up a better list.
We could always improve on anything that we receive, right?
That's the other thing that we think, the self thinks it can do.
It can always improve things, right?
But at some point we have to commit to something.
If we're always improving something before we commit to it, are we ever going to really commit to it?
Another quality of the Buddhist teachings that's interesting is that he had a fairly long teaching career, much longer than Jesus, I think much longer than Muhammad, but I don't really know.
The Buddha had a very responsive style, responding to his people's needs as he could understand them.
So he said very different things at different times and different places.
There's not really one sort of central Buddhist teaching.
Sometimes people say there is just to simplify and make it sound like a little more, I don't know what.
Well, like we often say that about the Four Noble Truths, which is a central Buddhist teaching, but it doesn't come up that often, actually.
It's in the very first sermon.
So we say a priori that must be the most important, but is it?
It's hard to know.
He had many different teachings.
One of the things they compared the Buddha to was like a doctor.

The Buddha was seen as like a doctor, and a doctor who is a skilled diagnostician—a skilled diagnostician, you know—just responds with the right teaching based on what they understand of the person's illness.
It's interesting to read the Buddha's teachings; they're sort of all over the place.
They're sort of repetitive.
It's sort of hard to get a handle on them because we want them to be very simple, very condensed.

But although his teachings are quite diverse and quite varied, and he especially used many different metaphors and similes, one one time, a different one another time, so although the expression was varied, the purpose was what was singular.
The purpose was what was really singular about the Buddha's teaching: the release from stress and suffering.
Then all the positive benefits that brings for each person and for all beings together when somebody is released from stress.
Released from a sort of, Anita, when she was here, it said it's like the mind builds walls around us.
She talked about different ways the mind builds walls.
It's released from these walls, from this prison.
So the Buddha was always speaking to that purpose.
He was famous for not wanting to answer questions that didn't really serve that purpose.
It's implied that he had this incredible enlightenment experience and some really deep insight into the nature of how the universe works.
So the implication is he maybe might've known the answer to some of the sort of more metaphorical or metaphysical or just sort of why questions, right?
We have that question, "Why?"
The Buddha mostly didn't answer if people said why.
He would stay silent or say something else.
He was interested in how.
We have this goal of a kind of freedom.
Of course, you can't really engage the path to anywhere unless you know where you're starting from.
That's why there's an emphasis in Buddhism on really understanding our experience as it is, very honestly.
That's why sometimes we hear people say, or we have this idea that Buddhism is like about suffering, it's about trouble.
I suppose that's true insofar as often our day-to-day life is about sort of avoiding the acknowledgement of the way things really are.
Maybe we need to bring up strongly one side to kind of wake people up, like, "Wow, you know, all is not right in Suffer City here."
But it's not really that life is suffering.
It's that we have to see life honestly and realistically so that we can walk on the path so we know where we're standing.
Try walking if you don't know where you're standing.
The Buddha's vision is much bigger than just you can learn some new tools and feel a little better.
His vision is actually complete release from stress and suffering, freedom in the middle of our life no matter what happens.
Part of the nature of our language is that it always divides things usually in two; it's just the nature of words.
You can't have the word good; it wouldn't mean anything if you didn't have the word bad.
The word small wouldn't mean anything if you didn't have the word large.
Our language, which we need, divides things into good and bad, what I like, what I don't like, and then most importantly, me and you.
Our language does this, and then our language is what our thoughts seem to more or less happen in.
Our thoughts seem to be somewhat symbolic and visual and somewhat linguistic.
People seem to vary a little bit there.

Part of this—prison sounds a little harsh—but part of the mechanism that we can be more free of is this process of dividing things up to the point that we ourselves are divided up, divided in half in some way.
The Buddha was not saying no pain, no coughing, no things not going the way you thought they would go.
He was saying it's possible to have freedom even then, even when it's going exactly the opposite way of what your consciousness predicted, which is so jarring for us, right?
We expect a very orderly universe, which seems to be another aspect of language.
We expect things to go the way they're going to go.
It doesn't go that way; it's surprising and shocking to us.
The vision of the Buddha is that even then, it's just the next moment.
We can be fully present and free in that moment and able to respond in that moment.
On the one hand, we start with suffering, and it's a big problem being a human being, and it is; we have to admit this, right?
It's pretty hard being a human being.
It's pretty hard being a person.
It's pretty hard making a living.
It's pretty hard having relationships.
It's pretty damn hard running a sangha, let me tell you.
We think that way, right?
We think that way.
At the same time, it's perfectly just exactly the way it is, right?
It's perfectly exactly the way it is.

That gap we see between, "Ah, it's hard," and "it's easy," seems to have to do with some wall there in between what it is and what it's supposed to be, or what we wanted it to be, or what we expected it to be, or what our parents told us it should be, something like this.
So there seems to be like this tiny gap that we can barely see or not see at all, which is like made of concrete, super kryptonite or something.
In one sense, the Buddhist path is how can we walk in a way that allows this tiny gap to finally close and to just be with life, with contentment and joy, no matter what it throws at us.
We feel far away and yet we're really close.
There are some apparent paradoxes and there is language that divides things into this and that.
makes it difficult to understand.

I think one of the greatest gifts of Buddhist logic and epistemology to the world is that we can change this habit, if we can work with this inner habit of it's this or it's that: I'm happy or I'm sad.
I like this or I don't like this.
You're my friend or you're not my friend.
What if we could turn that "or" into an "and," into an "and"?
So it's this and it's that: I'm happy and I'm sad.
You're my friend and not my friend.
Or maybe it's even more than that.
There are actually four steps in Buddhist logic.
It could be this and that.
Or what if it's not this and that?
What if it's not this and not that?
What if it's none of those?
Then where do you have left to stand?
So this list I want to bring up tonight is just a way of working with the mind, taking up different angles on this question of how do we divide the world?
How do we make walls?
How do we make experience as it is into suffering and pain?
That was the sort of the thrust of the Buddhist teaching: there's a method.
There are steps.
There's something you can actually do.
But then what happened in later Buddhism, which was a wonderful softening of that?
Because then the problem is that you say, okay, I get it.
I'm ill.
I have to work hard and do it right.
Follow the instructions and that will be better, right?
So then you have that, which maybe is true in a way, but maybe it creates new problems for us because then we have so much to do.
We have to work so hard and we might fail.
Later Buddhism also looked at the other side of this, which is that we're already complete.
That gap isn't even there; we made it up.
We're already whole.
So they have these ideas like Buddha nature and lots of different names for our wholeness.
That is what's emphasized in the Zen tradition.
I don't know if you've noticed, but there hasn't been a whole lot of instructions or steps or things to do around here in practice.
It's just sit down.
Follow the breath.
There are some instructions, you know.
You go to the teacher and some words are exchanged probably, but the Zen tradition emphasizes the side of wholeness, which is wonderful.
But it seems to me we need both: we need steps that we can actually take on the path, and a lived, felt understanding that we're already whole.
We're already complete.
We were never sick to begin with.
Dogen is always writing about that.
That's why we like to study Dogen.
As baffling as he is, it's because he's taking both of these sides at once.
And our mind, which wants it to be this way or that way, is like, what did he just say?
I got to read that paragraph again.
I don't get it.
So it's in everything we chant by him.
It's in everything we study.
When we studied Genjokoan last year, it's all through Genjokoan.
He often introduces a text by bringing up this point.
So like Fukanzazengi that we chant here on Saturdays sometimes, which is his kind of instruction manual for Zen practice, starts out this way:
*The way is basically perfect and all-pervading.
How could it be contingent upon practice and realization?
The Dharma vehicle is free and untrammeled.
What need is there for concentrated effort?
Indeed, the whole body is far beyond the world's dust.
It's already pure and perfect.
Who could believe in a means to brush it clean?
It's never apart from one, right where one is.
What is the use of going off here and there to practice?*
Remember chanting that?
And then he says, and yet, and yet, so it's always and yet, and yet if there's the slightest discrepancy, the way is as distant as heaven from earth.
If the least like or dislike arises, the mind is lost in confusion.
So there's preferences, right, from John's talk.

But even deeper than like preferences—and preferences is a perfectly good word for this—but preferences makes it sound like it's just sort of this mental baggage, like I have too many preferences, if only I had less preferences, I could just sort of be better.
But it seems to be a much deeper thing than that, right?
It's down to our roots, you know.
It's like not quite believing that everything's okay.
Not quite believing that the Dharma vehicle is free, untrammeled, pure, and that we are the Dharma vehicle already.
What's wonderful about Zen is we can actually have experiences in Zazen every time.
We don't always even notice them, but these moments, these moments when everything is just at rest, it's just fine, maybe just for an instant, or a breath, or a day of sesshin, or who knows.
So it's this kind of funny thing, how do we hold these two things that seem sort of a little bit at odds with each other?
On the one hand, you're fine the way you are; things are complete, just kind of let go of this idea that something's wrong, you know.
On the one hand, the other hand, things are not right, you know.
Human beings got wired up in a funny way.
We need to do some very skillful, very wise discernment, very steady effort.
We need to work.
We need to actually make an effort.
And these things at the same time.
I've been enjoying a book.
I brought it in.
Sometimes it's really good to read a book that's written in a nice simple way.
I've been enjoying this book called *The Wide Awake: A Buddhist Guide for Teens*.
We should all read this book, actually.
It's on the Brooklyn Zen Center reading list.
I was hearing about how they use this in Brooklyn.
I said, okay, I'll read it.
And it's great.
It's a very clear book on the practice.
I feel like I'm just mumbling because this woman is just very clear.
There's lots of examples about boyfriends and girlfriends too, which is fun because for teens.
It's a very clear book.
I wanted to share with you the way her name is Diana Winston.
I wanted to share with you the way she kind of describes and works with this apparent dichotomy between the work we have to do and the ways that we just need to let go.
No work.
So she writes:
*In Buddhism, we talk about the potential for becoming enlightened or a fully waking up.
But what does this mean?
In the Buddhist tradition, the Sanskrit word nirvana is used to mean a state of full awakening.
The word literally means coolness and is associated with peace and freedom.
Nirvana is seen as the ultimate goal of Buddhism.
What the Buddha achieves under the Bodhi tree is nirvana.
However, many misconceptions surround the words nirvana and enlightenment.

Some people imagine if I reach enlightenment, the world will explode into white light or I'll become one with everyone or I'll have omniscience and know how to help all beings on the planet or all my problems will be solved or I'll be extremely powerful and loved.
Some schools of Buddhism say every time we have a moment of awakening like those moments of self-awareness when we're fully present here and now, we're having a little nirvana.
And in that case, to reach nirvana, all we have to do is practice waking up in our lives as much as possible, moment after moment, time after time.
The late Thai master Ajahn Buddhadasa who coined the phrase little nirvana said, nirvana can be present here and now by taking your breath in cool and letting it out cool.
It is the realm that cools down the heart, quenches the thirst and extinguishes the suffering existing in our daily life.
Automatically, without us necessarily being conscious of it, it really is a nourishing process for all, for our life all the time.
And know how he says, not necessarily conscious of it.
So it's not just like the little me working here.*
Anyway, she goes on.
Another Buddhist school considers nirvana to be the eradication of three mental weeds: greed, hatred, and delusion.
These nasty plants grow in our minds and upon enlightenment are finally ripped out by their roots and never grow again.
In their place, generosity, love, and wisdom thrive.
They say that the plant is uprooted in stages, a little at a time, more like weeding a garden over many seasons for many years.
So other schools of Buddhism say that the truth is we're already enlightened.
It is our true nature, but we have forgotten.
Often this existing enlightenment is called our Buddha nature, the whole radiant inner self that cannot be changed by anything external.
In some traditions, our minds are compared to the vast blue sky, extending as far as the eye can see.
However, clouds and rainstorms can pass by and cover our true nature.

Zen master Hakuen said, although there are countless teachings that instruct us how to obtain enlightenment, the ultimate instruction is there is no teaching that is superior to the true practice of awakening to one's own nature.
Let me read Hakuen again.

*Although there are countless teachings that instruct us how to obtain enlightenment, the ultimate instruction is there is no teaching that is superior to the true practice of awakening to one's true nature, one's own nature.* Diana Winston goes on, how do we make sense of these seemingly contradictory teachings?
If I'm already enlightened, why do spiritual practice?
Or if I have a lot of work to do to free my mind from greed, hate, and delusion, how could I already be enlightened?
I like to hold the two views together.
On the one hand, I diligently practice meditation and waking up in daily life while remembering the incredible human potential for full awakening.
Imagine, imagine, this is an imagination thing.
One day, my mind may be completely free of greed, hatred, and delusion.
As I practice, I get more and more taste of free mind.
On the other hand, as I develop my spiritual path, I remember that an awakened heart and mind is true human nature.
How could it be otherwise?
I try to accept myself exactly as I am.
I remind myself that even if I don't feel enlightened, even if I don't feel enlightened, being awake is the natural condition of mind, which I can experience from time to time.
And through practice, increasingly more often, I feel this: whatever I encounter on my path, no matter how challenging, cannot possibly cover up the pure radiance of my heart.
And so as we'll see when I finally spring this list on you, faith is in there, faith is in there.
This faith in the teaching, in our true heart, in whatever you want to call it, seems to be a condition for engaging with this stepping, this steady practice.

One of the things I've done to kind of explore this teaching, I've read a couple of books and I did list—we're going to talk about this, continue talking about this a lot, and we're going to talk about it in the study retreat.
Hopefully, I won't get too tired of it, but in the description on the website of the study retreat, I describe what the books are.
So if you want to look up the books, I won't tell you now, because who remembers these things?
But I got books in two very different traditions, which is neat.
One is by a Chinese Chan master, and the other is by an American monk in the Thai forest tradition.
So very different parts of Buddhism.
Appreciate this list.
And so in addition to just studying it and reading the commentaries and trying to explore this in my life, and some of these lists I'd studied before, I concocted a practice, a home practice.
Because one of the things I've really come to appreciate about our ritual practice is the way there's a way it seems to plant seeds in the mind.
You chant something over and over and over again, like that Dogen piece sort of gets in there ready to pop out when you need it.

And I thought that would be a great way for us to kind of make these lists come alive, not just read them or talk about them, but to chant them and bow with them and recite them and bring them forward as objects of spiritual practice and spiritual power.
So I want to end my talk with a little chanting and bowing, and then I'll hand out the list at the very end, okay?
Let's all stand up.
Let's do, you know, how we do the kind of staggered cushion thing for the full moon ceremony.
Natalis can just model how to do that.
We're going to do a bunch of prostrations, so it's good to have a mat.
This row, along with me, you just pull the cushion one width over, and the fourth one, do the same thing.
Stand right behind it, facing the front.
Yeah, standing behind the cushion, facing the front.
With your bowing, you see you want your shoulder all pushed off the mat.
So this is what I could come to.
I don't know if this is traditional practice or not.
The commentaries by Chan Master Shenxiu talked about we're doing lots of bowing, so I'm going to assume that this is perfectly great if there's anything to do with it.
So when you hear the bell, we're bowing.
And if it's too much to do all the prostrations, there is that on there.
We're going to just do standing bow.
We venerate the three treasures and give thanks for this path of training and practice.
We bow to practice the aids to awakening with our whole hearts, bodies, and minds continuously throughout day and night for the benefit of all beings.

The 37 A's to awakening are the four foundations of mindfulness: the mindfulness of the body, the mindfulness of sensations and reactions, the mindfulness of thoughts and emotions, the patterns and habits; the four proper exertions against unwholesome states: regarding abandoning unwholesome states, cultivating wholesome states, maintaining wholesome states; the four bases of freedom: the concentration of desire, the concentration of persistence, the concentration of intention, the concentration of discrimination; the five wholesome roots: the root of faith, diligence, mindfulness; the root of samadhi, of wisdom; the five wholesome strengths: the strength of faith, the strength of diligence, the strength of mindfulness, the strength of samadhi, the strength of wisdom; the seven factors of enlightenment: the factor of mindfulness, the factor of discernment, the factor of diligence, the factor of lightness and ease, the factor of samadhi, the factor of equanimity; the noble, the path of action, the path of effort, the path of rights of mindfulness, the path of samadhi, and our vow to practice the 37 steps of the Bodhi, Paksika, Dharma.
May the benefit of this ongoing practice bring joy, wisdom, and understanding for ourselves and all beings in all directions.
May we, through this patient effort, enter the fullness of Buddha's way.

Should send you with a pedometer. I'll probably like max it out. And to try to take each step, you know, each step of that journey as a step on the path. You know, seven people signed up. Isn't that amazing? Never done this before. So thank you to Bob for being sort of nutty enough to say yes to that.

Because you never know who's going to respond, right? That's the other thing about walking on the path, is if you take a step on the path, you don't know. We think we're so self-focused, right? Think about it. We're so self-focused. We think about, well, is this good for me? But then we step onto the path because we think it's good for us

and maybe it is. But then maybe we look over our shoulder and we see, oh, we helped somebody else take a step on the path.
